title: Probability and base rates
note: Probabilities run from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Independent events do not affect each other, so past coin flips do not change the next one. Bayes' theorem, in plain words: start from the base rate (the prior), then raise or lower it by how much more likely the evidence is if the hypothesis is true than if it is false.

read.title: Bayes in plain words
text: Suppose a trait occurs in 1 person in 1,000, and a test for it is 99% accurate: it catches 99% of people who have the trait and wrongly flags 1% of people who do not. You test positive. How likely is it that you have the trait? Most people guess about 99%. The answer is about 9%.

Picture 100,000 people. About 100 have the trait, and the test flags about 99 of them. Of the 99,900 who lack it, 1% is about 999 false positives. So roughly 1,098 people test positive, and only 99 of them have the trait. The rare trait's low base rate swamps the test's accuracy.

This is the heart of Bayes' theorem. Start with the prior probability, here 1 in 1,000. Then ask how much more likely the evidence is if the hypothesis is true than if it is false. A positive result is 99 times likelier with the trait than without it, which raises the odds a great deal, but from a very low starting point.

Ignoring the starting point is base rate neglect. A related slip is confusing the probability of a positive test given the trait with the probability of the trait given a positive test. They are different numbers.

q.q: In the example, about what fraction of positive results are true positives?
Why is the answer so low?
o: The trait's base rate is very low

q.q: What does Bayes' theorem combine, per the reading?
o: The prior and how strongly the evidence favors the hypothesis
